name: Basic Hermeneutics (Principles of Interpretation)
path: New Testament Studies: Life and Doctrine in Christ

objectives.text: Identify Jesus as the one the whole Bible points to and tells about
Retell a Bible story in order by naming who was in it, what happened, and what it shows about God
Name the Bible as God's Word, written by people whom God's Spirit guided
Recall that God gives his Word to tell us what to believe about him and how he wants us to live
Answer the question of what a Bible passage teaches about God using details from the passage
Explain how the verses before and after a passage help show what it means
Distinguish what a passage meant to its first hearers from how it applies to readers today
Identify the author, first audience, and purpose of a New Testament book using clues within the text
Compare how a Gospel, a historical narrative, a letter, and apocalyptic writing are each read
Apply the principle that Scripture interprets Scripture by using a clearer passage to explain a harder one
Use cross-references and a concordance to locate passages related to a text being studied
Analyze a passage using the steps of observation, interpretation, and application
Identify figures of speech such as metaphor, simile, and hyperbole in Jesus' teaching and explain their intended meaning
Interpret a parable by identifying its main point in light of its setting and audience rather than as historical narrative
Explain how cultural and historical background clarifies the meaning of a text without overriding what the text says
Analyze an example of a verse taken out of context and show how its context corrects the misreading
Trace the argument of a paragraph in an epistle by identifying connecting words such as therefore, because, and so that
Explain how New Testament writers read Old Testament passages as fulfilled in Christ
Distinguish descriptive passages that report what happened from prescriptive passages that command what should be done
Conduct a word study that determines a word's meaning from its use in context rather than from its root alone
Construct an exegetical outline that shows the structure and main idea of a New Testament passage
Explain the Reformed teaching that the Holy Spirit illumines readers to understand Scripture while careful study remains necessary
Evaluate competing interpretations of a passage using context, genre, and the analogy of Scripture
Defend the Reformed doctrine of the perspicuity of Scripture for what is necessary to salvation
Explain the Reformed view that creeds and confessions guide interpretation while remaining subordinate to Scripture as the supreme judge
Compare the grammatical-historical method with allegorical and reader-centered approaches to interpretation
Write an interpretation of a New Testament passage that applies the grammatical-historical method from observation through application

changes: Kept and reworded real competencies: Jesus as the Bible's focus, the Bible as God's Word, believing and obeying, asking what a text teaches about God, then versus now, context, genre comparison, Scripture interprets Scripture, OIA, parables, background, out-of-context dangers, exegetical outline, evaluating interpretations, perspicuity, and grammatical-historical method. Recast the grade 12 synthesis item as two concrete tasks: comparing methods and writing an interpretation. Added missing skills: retelling narrative, finding author, audience and purpose, cross-reference tools, figures of speech, tracing epistle arguments, NT use of the OT, descriptive versus prescriptive passages, word studies, illumination, and the place of confessions under Scripture. Cultural background is framed only as an interpretive principle so historical content stays with the sibling sub-topics. Moved the then-versus-now item to grade 4 and added confessional anchors (WSC Q2-3, WCF 1.4, 1.6, 1.7, 1.9, 1.10) along with verse-level Scripture references.
